trigger: Fee proposal drafting and consultant coordination ahead of an office move

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Grace Kim, thanks for speaking with me. I have Banksia Architects as a forty-four person studio in Fitzroy, and you manage studio operations, is that right?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Yes. We're moving office next quarter, and pulling the studio apart has shown how much of our process lives in people's heads. I'm gathering options before the directors decide what to fund for the new financial year.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: What is taking the most time across the studio right now?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Fee proposals. Every new project starts with one, and each takes a director and me two or three days. We pull scope from the client brief, stages from a template nobody fully trusts, rates from a spreadsheet, and consultant allowances from the last similar job.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: How many of those go out in a year, and who writes them?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Somewhere near ninety. Three directors write them, I chase the pieces, and our practice accountant checks the numbers at the end. About a third are for repeat clients where most of the content already exists in a proposal we then cannot find.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Where do the finished proposals and the consultant information actually sit?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Proposals are in project folders on the shared drive, named however the director felt that week. Consultant quotes arrive by email and stay there. The fee spreadsheet lives on somebody's desktop. There is no single place you could ask what we charged for a similar school project.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: And what does the consultant coordination side look like once a project is running?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Chasing, mostly. We coordinate structural, services, planning and landscape consultants, each with their own deadlines and drawing sets. A large part of my week is working out who owes what. When a date slips, nobody finds out until the coordination meeting.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: If the directors funded one thing, what would you want fixed first, and who makes that call?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Fee proposals, without question, because they gate every new job. The two senior directors decide together. One is focused on winning work, the other has been watching every dollar since we signed the new lease.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: That is a clean first build. A short paid discovery phase to map how a proposal is actually assembled, then a fixed-scope build of a drafting agent that pulls scope, stages, rates and consultant allowances out of your own past projects. For a studio your size that lands near $66,400, and the agents and prompts are handed over to you at the end.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: That is the right problem, but I should be honest with you. The directors will not sign anything until the fit-out budget is settled. We have already committed to the lease, the joinery and a fit-out consultant, and there is not much appetite for anything else this side of the move.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: That is fair, and I am not going to push a proposal at directors who have not seen the problem framed yet. I will send a short findings note and a fee proposal workflow map so you have something concrete to put in front of them when the budget conversation opens.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: That would help. I can get a page read. I cannot get a meeting in the diary for something they have not yet agreed is worth funding.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Understood. The note will separate what a build would change from what you could tighten yourselves for nothing, so it does not read as a pitch.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Please keep that split honest. If every line points at hiring someone, the director watching cash will stop reading at the second paragraph and the whole thing dies there.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Would it be worth putting a date in now for a session with both directors once the note has landed?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: I would rather not. I do not know when the fit-out budget gets signed off, and booking something they have not asked for tends to backfire here.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Then I will leave the timing with you entirely. Send me a line when the budget lands and we can pick it up from wherever it sits then.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: That works. Realistically it is after the move, so October at the earliest.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: That is fine by me. The findings note does not go stale, and the workflow map is useful to you even if you never engage us to build anything.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: That is the part I actually want. Nobody has ever written down how a proposal gets made, so every director does it differently and I am the one reconciling three versions of the truth.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: That is usually where most of the saving sits. Before any agent exists, getting three directors to agree on one assembly order takes a real chunk out of the two or three days you described.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: You will not get three directors to agree on anything by email, but a map they can argue over in a room might get there.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: I will keep it to one page for exactly that reason, with the consultant coordination piece noted separately as a possible second phase rather than folded into the same number.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Good. If you bundle coordination into the same figure, the director watching cash will treat the whole thing as scope creep before he has worked out what it does.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Noted. One problem, one number, and everything else listed as a later option they can ignore.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Grace Kim
turns.text: Thanks Sam. I am genuinely interested, I just need the internal timing to catch up with it.
